newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana announces re-introduction of VAT in budget.
newsitem.headline: Ghana announces re-introduction of VAT in budget.

text.p: The Ghana government submitted its 1997 budget to parliament on Wednesday, announcing the re-introduction of Value Added Tax which sparked riots in 1995.
The opposition which holds 66 of the 199 assembly seats, boycotted the session. It insisted Finance Minister Kwame Peprah be vetted by parliament before being confirmed as minister.
In May 1995 the hasty introduction of VAT led to a wave of price increases, touching off mass demonstrations in which five were shot dead. The government withdrew the tax.

"Government must have the strength and courage to take the tough decision necessary for the good governance of the country," Peprah said before announcing that a new VAT bill would be brought before parliament this year.
The VAT law would not come into force until January 1, 1998, to allow more time for public education.
"It is our determination to achieve a higher growth this year by increasing food supply, enhancing value added in domestic production and generating further employment," Peprah told lawmakers.
Government would also take measures to improve upon the fiscal and monetary performance and further reduce inflation.

The 1997 macroeconomic targets are a real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 5.5 percent, an inflation rate of 15 percent, a government budget surplus of 191.2 billion cedis ($108.3 million) and a balance of payments surplus of $100 million.

The 1997 budget projects revenue of 2,944.3 billion cedis (23.4 percent of GDP) and spending at 2,753.1 billion cedis. The 1996 figures were 2,268.5 billion and 2,410.5 billion, representing a deficit of 142 billion cedis (one percent of GDP), instead of the projected 158.7 billion surplus.

"New salary levels negotiated led to a higher than programmed wage bill, while non-disbursement of programmed foreign inflows of $60 million presented obstacles to the projected surplus," said Peprah.

Improved food supply and a slower a rate of depreciation of the cedi helped push down inflation from 70.8 percent in December 1995 to 32.6 percent in December 1996, although it remained 12.6 points above the targeted 20 percent.
Peprah said Ghana's GDP grew by 5.2 percent in 1996, compared to 4.5 percent in 1995. Annual population growth is about three percent, according to World Bank data.
